Tell your manager about your first impressions of a new team (real or imagined) and propose one change, with at least four cleft sentences.
exercicios.frase: What
exercicios.resposta: What surprised me most was how friendly everyone is. What works well is the Monday meeting. What doesn't work is file sharing: the reason why we lose time is that everyone uses a different system. What I'd suggest is one shared folder. All I'm asking for is one afternoon.

exercicios.enunciado: Is it better to propose big changes in your first months in a new job, or to wait until you know the place? Why?
exercicios.frase: The reason why
exercicios.resposta: I'd wait a little. The reason why is simple: in the first months, you don't know why things are done in a certain way. What I'd do is take notes, ask questions, and propose one small change first.

Tell the story of a success at work, at school or in your community, and correct one common misunderstanding about why it worked. Use It was… that / who…, It wasn't… it was…, and one emphatic do or did.
exercicios.frase: It was
exercicios.resposta: Last year our school's results improved a lot. Everyone thinks it was the new computers that made the difference. But it wasn't the computers — it was the extra reading hour every morning. It was our director who insisted on it. The computers did help, but much less.

exercicios.enunciado: When a project succeeds, who usually gets the credit, and who should? Why?
exercicios.frase: who
exercicios.resposta: Usually it's the manager who gets the credit. But it's often the people on the ground who did the real work. A good manager does take responsibility for failures, and shares the credit for successes.

That's not true. Look at the numbers.

Make the case for one change in your workplace, school or town. Then answer: "We tried something like that before, and it didn't work." Concede, reformulate, turn it around and come back to your point.
exercicios.frase: grant you
exercicios.resposta: What I'm proposing is a weekly English club at lunch. I'll grant you that a course failed three years ago. If I understand you correctly, your concern is that people won't come. But that course was in the evening. Which is exactly why I'd start with thirty minutes at lunch.

exercicios.enunciado: Is it a good idea to ask a colleague to play devil's advocate before an important meeting? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: Yes, because it's much better to hear the hard questions from a friend than from the board. What a devil's advocate gives you is time to prepare your answers.

Make the case for a product, a project or an idea you believe in: its main selling point, the benefit, one objection you would address, and the bottom line.
exercicios.frase: bottom line
exercicios.resposta: I'd like to make the case for solar water heaters in school kitchens. The main selling point is cost: they pay for themselves in about two years. The usual objection is the initial price, and that's fair. But the bottom line is simple: it's the cheapest hot water they'll ever have.

exercicios.enunciado: What persuades you more: numbers or stories? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: Stories catch my attention, but numbers make me decide. What works best is a short story with one strong number, because I remember the story and I trust the number.

opcoes.texto: Her strongest point came too late.

exercicios.enunciado: How many shops use ShopPay?

exercicios.frase: This is Kwabena. It wasn't banks that taught us this. It was the shop owners in Soweto, who told us what they needed.
exercicios.enunciado: Who taught Kwabena what small shops need?

exercicios.enunciado: What does Elena's device do?

opcoes.texto: It alerts the family when a person's normal day changes.
It calls an ambulance every day.

exercicios.frase: This is Elena. I understand why you'd say that. But consider this: the grandmother decides who sees the data.
exercicios.enunciado: How does Elena answer the "spying" objection?

opcoes.texto: The grandmother decides who sees the data.

Kwabena answers the jury: "I'll grant you that they could." He is…

opcoes.texto: conceding before coming back to his point

You are on the jury. Say which pitch you would choose to win, and why, and give one piece of advice to each founder.
exercicios.frase: What made
exercicios.resposta: I'd choose Kwabena. What made his pitch strong was the first sentence: in five seconds, I knew the problem and the solution. My advice to Thato: start with the twenty percent. To Elena: the idea is terrific, but the privacy answer should be in the pitch itself.

exercicios.enunciado: Should a pitch start with a number, a story or a problem? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: With a problem, I think, because people only care about a solution when they feel the problem. Then a number shows it's real. A story is great too, but it must be very short.

Defend a proposal of your own before a sceptical director: the main idea in one sentence, one proof with a cleft sentence, answers to "It's too expensive" and "It won't last", and a smaller request at the end.
exercicios.frase: All I'm asking
exercicios.resposta: What our office needs is a small solar system for the server room. Last year, it was the power cuts that stopped our work. That's a fair point: it isn't cheap, but we spend more on diesel. I'll grant you batteries don't last forever. All I'm asking for is a six-month trial.

exercicios.enunciado: Present these results in English, with two numbers and one comment: "Inquérito aos clientes (120 respostas): 76% compram cá todas as semanas; 58% querem pagar com o telemóvel; queixa principal: as filas ao sábado (44%). Comentário: 'Gosto de cá vir, mas ao sábado desisto.'"
exercicios.frase: customers
exercicios.resposta: We asked a hundred and twenty customers. About three quarters shop here every week, and more than half want to pay by phone. The main complaint is the Saturday queues. One comment says it all: "I like coming here, but on Saturdays I give up."
exercicios.contexto: Mediação: dois números e uma voz real.

Make the case for one change in your workplace, school or town. What's the strongest argument against it, and how would you answer it?
exercicios.frase: What
exercicios.resposta: What our town needs is a night bus to the hospital. The reason why is simple: nurses finish at midnight and walk home in the dark. The strongest objection is cost. That's a fair point. But consider this: one accident costs more than a year of buses.

exercicios.enunciado: A colleague says: "Your idea won't work. People won't change." Answer with a concession and a cleft sentence.
exercicios.frase: fair point
exercicios.resposta: That's a fair point — people don't like change. But it isn't the change they dislike, it's being forced. What I'm proposing is a three-month trial, and anyone can say no.
